stem: Which branch of government makes the laws of Zimbabwe?

options.content: The legislature, which is the Parliament of Zimbabwe
The executive, which is led by the President
options.rationale: The executive carries out the laws.

options.content: The judiciary, which is made up of all the courts
The police, who are part of the security services of the state

explanation: Parliament, the legislature, makes laws; the executive carries them out and the judiciary interprets them.

stem: What is representative democracy?

options.content: Citizens elect people to make laws and decisions for them
options.rationale: Correct: this is the usual form in modern states.

options.content: Citizens vote on every law themselves in one large gathering
A single party chooses the leaders without any vote by citizens
Leaders are chosen at birth from a few families in the country

explanation: In a representative democracy citizens elect representatives to make laws and decisions on their behalf.

stem: How many members does the Senate of Zimbabwe have under the 2013 Constitution?

options.rationale: Sixty are elected by provinces; the total is larger.
This is the number of constituency seats in the National Assembly.
Correct: 60 elected, 16 chiefs and 4 other members.
This is the National Assembly total with the women's quota.

explanation: The Senate has 80 members: six from each of ten provinces, 16 chiefs, two members for persons with disabilities, and the President and Deputy President of the National Council of Chiefs.

stem: Why is the separation of powers important in a democracy?

options.content: It allows the President to make laws, enforce them and judge cases at the same time
It makes sure that Parliament may overrule every decision of the courts at will
It removes the need for any elections because the courts choose the leaders
It stops one body from holding all the power and allows each to check the others
options.rationale: Correct: it spreads and limits power.

explanation: Dividing government into three branches prevents the concentration of power and allows checks on abuse.

stem: What is the role of the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission (ZEC)?

options.content: To appoint every minister and decide how the Cabinet will vote
To hear appeals against the decisions of the Constitutional Court
options.rationale: The Constitutional Court is the final authority.

options.content: To register voters, run elections and announce the final results
options.rationale: Correct: it is an independent commission.

options.content: To write the laws that Parliament must pass each year without change

explanation: ZEC is an independent commission that registers voters, conducts elections and announces results.
hints: Its name tells you what it manages.

stem: What does devolution mean?

options.content: Giving all power to the President and the Cabinet in the capital city
Moving the national capital from one city to another city in the country
options.rationale: That has nothing to do with devolution.

options.content: Abolishing local councils and provincial governors altogether, for ever
Sharing power and resources with provincial and local levels of government

explanation: Devolution transfers some powers and resources from the national government to provinces and local authorities; the Constitution sets at least 5 per cent of revenue for them.
hints: Think of power moving down from the centre.

stem: Which example shows the judiciary acting as a check on the other branches?

options.content: Parliament passes the budget for the coming financial year after debate
The Constitutional Court declares a law to be unconstitutional and invalid
The President appoints a new Cabinet and Vice-Presidents after an election
Citizens vote for their representatives in a general election
options.rationale: This is the exercise of citizens' rights.

explanation: Courts can declare laws and executive acts unconstitutional, which limits both Parliament and the executive.
hints: Which action involves courts reviewing others' acts?

stem: Which statement about democracy in Zimbabwe in practice is best supported?

options.content: All observers and parties have agreed that every election was free and fair
The Constitution sets up checks and rights, but views differ on how well they work
options.rationale: Correct: it gives the framework and the dispute.

options.content: The Constitution has no provisions on elections, courts or Parliament
No citizen has ever been able to take part in public hearings or petitions

explanation: The framework is detailed, but observers, parties and the government have judged the practice differently.
hints: Choose the statement that records both the framework and the debate.

stem: In a direct democracy citizens vote on decisions themselves.
explanation: Referendums are an example of direct democracy.

stem: Under the 2013 Constitution the President may serve only two five-year terms.
explanation: The Constitution limits the President to two terms of five years each.

stem: In the separation of powers the judiciary makes the laws and Parliament interprets them.
explanation: Parliament makes laws and the judiciary interprets them and settles disputes.

stem: Match each organ or term to its role.

right.content: Interprets the law and settles disputes
Carries out the law and runs the government
Makes laws and scrutinises the executive

explanation: These are the organs of government and the electoral commission.

stem: Put these events in chronological order.

left.content: The first elections on the basis of universal adult suffrage
The Global Political Agreement leads to a Government of National Unity
A referendum approves the new Constitution

stem: Describe the characteristics of a democracy.

points.description: Regular free and fair elections with universal adult suffrage
Competition between political parties and a free media
The rule of law and an independent judiciary
Protection of human rights and accountability of leaders

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A democracy holds regular free and fair elections in which all adults can vote. Political parties compete and the media are free, the rule of law applies with an independent judiciary, and human rights are protected and leaders are accountable.

explanation: One mark for each characteristic described.

stem: Explain the importance of the separation of powers.

points.description: It prevents any one person or body from holding all the power, which reduces the risk of abuse
Each branch can check the others, for example courts can strike down unconstitutional laws and Parliament can question ministers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Separation of powers prevents any one person or body from holding all the power, which reduces the risk of abuse. Each branch can check the others, for example the courts can strike down unconstitutional laws and Parliament can question ministers.

explanation: Credit developed reasons with an example.
hints: Give a reason about power and an example of a check.

stem: Explain how devolution may improve democracy.

points.description: It brings decisions about services closer to the people who are affected, so they can take part and hold local leaders to account
It shares resources more fairly between regions, with at least 5 per cent of national revenue set aside, which can reduce the feeling of exclusion

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Devolution brings decisions about local services closer to the people affected, so they can take part and hold local leaders to account. It shares resources more fairly between regions, with at least 5 per cent of national revenue set aside, which can reduce the feeling of exclusion.

explanation: Credit developed reasons.
hints: Think about participation and about the sharing of resources.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a comment by a fictional constitutional lawyer in a weekly newspaper, 2018 (invented for this question)

> On paper the 2013 Constitution is admirable. It limits the President to two terms, separates the powers, creates independent commissions and promises devolution. The test is whether those who hold office are willing to be bound by it, and whether the commissions are given the funds and the freedom to do their work.

**Source B** — a speech by a fictional provincial councillor at a community meeting, 2019 (invented for this question)

> For decades decisions about our clinic and our road were made in the capital. Now the law says that a share of the national revenue belongs to the provinces. We shall hold our leaders to account for how it is spent, and we expect to see the results in our wards.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What features of the Constitution does Source A praise?

points.description: A two-term limit for the President and separation of powers
Independent commissions and the promise of devolution

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What does Source B expect from devolution?

points.description: A share of national revenue for the provinces to spend on local needs such as the clinic and road
Local leaders held to account and results in the wards

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How far do the sources agree about the working of the Constitution?

points.description: Agree that the Constitution gives a good framework and raises expectations of accountability
Differ in tone: A doubts whether leaders will be bound and whether commissions will be funded; B is hopeful that devolution will bring results
Provenance: A is a lawyer's analysis for readers of a newspaper; B a councillor speaking to supporters at a local meeting
Own knowledge: devolution and alignment of laws have been gradual, and views differ

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources agree that the Constitution sets out a good framework and that leaders must be held to account. They differ in tone. Source A, a lawyer writing for a newspaper, doubts whether office-holders will be bound by the Constitution and whether commissions will be funded, while Source B, a councillor speaking to a local meeting, is hopeful that devolution will bring visible results. My own knowledge suggests that devolution and alignment of laws have been gradual and that views differ on the pace.

explanation: Both sources are invented: a lawyer's comment and a councillor's speech.
hints: For (c), compare the doubt in A with the hope in B.

stem: To what extent has Zimbabwe promoted democracy since 1980?

points.description: Framework: universal suffrage from 1980, regular elections, the 2013 Constitution, separation of powers, independent commissions
Participation: constitution-making outreach and referendum, public hearings, women's quota, devolution
Criticisms: dominance of the executive, delays in aligning laws, limits on media and assembly, disputes about elections and the voters' roll; the government's response
Different views and change over time
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Zimbabwe has promoted democracy in important ways, but views differ on how fully it has been achieved. Since 1980 all adults have been able to vote, elections have been held regularly, and the 2013 Constitution, approved by referendum after wide consultation, set out a separation of powers, term limits, independent commissions, a quota of seats for women and a plan for devolution. Citizens can take part through public hearings, parties and civil society. Critics say that the executive remains dominant, that laws were slow to be aligned with the Constitution, that media and assembly are restricted and that some elections were disputed over the voters' roll and violence. The government replies that it has followed the law, that the courts are open, and that devolution is being phased in. I conclude that the framework for democracy has developed considerably, but the extent to which it works in practice is contested and depends on the independence of institutions.

explanation: Credit framework, participation, criticisms, different views and a supported judgement.
hints: Compare the formal framework with how it works, and use different viewpoints.

stem: Assess the importance of the independence of the judiciary in a democracy such as Zimbabwe.

points.description: Role: interprets the Constitution, protects rights, settles disputes between citizens and the state
Independence: judges are subject only to the Constitution and the law, the Judicial Service Commission
Limits: pressure on courts, resources, perceptions of independence, dependence on enforcement by the executive
Judgement on how important independence is

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; balance is attempted and a judgement is reached, but it is only partly supported or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: An independent judiciary is essential to democracy because it interprets the Constitution, protects rights and settles disputes between citizens and the state without fear or favour. The Constitution requires judges to be subject only to the Constitution and the law and uses the Judicial Service Commission to help protect independence. But courts can be affected by pressure, limited resources and the need for the executive to carry out their orders, and perceptions of independence vary. I conclude that independence is one of the most important safeguards of democracy, because without it the other checks on power are weak.

explanation: Credit explained role, limits and a judgement.
hints: Link independence to the protection of rights and the limiting of power.
